extracted.intended_audience: writers, screenwriters, students and scholars studying narrative/dramatic structure
extracted.subtask_description: A catalog of named story/dramatic-structure models and their component parts, describing how plots, acts, and emotional arcs can be arranged for fiction, drama, and screenwriting. Useful for writers and analysts choosing or evaluating a structural model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kwik Kwak (crick crack) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves three elements: the narrator, the protagonist, and the audience; the story is considered a performance with synergy among these elements; the narrator may draw attention to the narrative or to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure often includes telling riddles to test the audience, audience acting as chorus and commenting, and usually a ritual ending. Emphasizes performance, audience participation, and narrator visibility as structural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Griot storytelling structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral West African storytelling form used by griot storytellers (e.g., Anansi tales) with memory/collective knowledge as central driver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical structure: Opening formula (jokes and riddles to engage audience, then a solemn beginning); Body/expository section (narration, setting up characters, defining conflict, with singing, dancing, shouting, inviting audience participation; language full of images and symbolism); Conclusive formula (closure and moral). Storyteller functions as educator/counselor/entertainer/custodian of memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robleto
rubrics_metrics.description: Nicaraguan story form made of: Line of Repetition, Introduction, Climax, Journeys, Close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic/folk form emphasizing repetition and journey motifs; uses those named components as formal signposts for structuring a tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harawi (Andean lyric/genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional Andean song/lyric genre often moody, soulful, slow and melodic; words speak of love, peasants' plight, orphans' privations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure and atmosphere are dominated by mood and melodic form (minor pentatonic scale); structural guidance is stylistic rather than plot-based—focus on evocative atmosphere and thematic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream diary / Dream record structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms that begin with or center on a dream; dream diary (Japan) records and shares dreams; Dream record (Ming Dynasty) starts with a dream and deals with a character reflecting on life or telling another dead character about life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used for reflection, regret, acceptance, or movement through memory; can be used to structure narratives that focus on inner life, retrospection, and acceptance arcs rather than external action.

rubrics_metrics.name: East Asian 4-act (Kishōtenketsu)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally Chinese qǐ chéng zhuǎn hé; in Japanese kishōtenketsu: four-part structure (introduction, development, twist/turn, conclusion) adapted differently across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes development and turn without necessarily centering on conflict; provides formal act divisions useful for pacing and thematic development in East Asian narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eight‑legged essay constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigid Ming/Qing dynasty essay form required in imperial examinations; candidates must conform to standards and not write innovatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests coherent writing and basic logic; forbids creative/innovative expression—serves as an example of a prescriptive formal constraint that shapes content and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jo‑ha‑kyū rhythm/principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese concept of modulation: 'beginning, break, rapid'—actions should begin slowly, speed up, then end swiftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied across arts including dramatic structure and collaborative verse; recommended as a pacing principle for movement and tension across sections of a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chiastic (chiastic structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of repetition and mirror structure (A B C B' A') found in sacred texts like Torah, Bible, Quran.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for organizing material around a central point by mirroring elements outward from that center; emphasizes symmetry and thematic return rather than linear progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hakawati (palestinian/Arabian storytelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A traditional Palestinian/Arab storytelling form which includes frame-story traditions such as One Thousand and One Nights and many religious works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often uses embedded narratives and frame devices; structure supports oral performance and multiple nested tales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Karagöz shadow-play four-part structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Karagöz plays are structured in four parts: Mukaddime (Introduction), Muhavere (dialogue between Karagöz and Hacivat), Fasil (main plot), Bitiş (conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mukaddime includes semai/recitation and comic entrance; Bitiş ends with a short argument and stock lines. Guidance: use stock interaction patterns, musical/recitative elements, and a formal concluding exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ta'ziyeh ritual structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Iranian Shi'ite ritual reenacting the death of Husayn ibn Ali; a dramatized ritual with religious/moral function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure and content are determined by ritual/religious requirements—useful example of storytelling where form serves communal/memorial purposes rather than entertainment alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: One‑act play form
rubrics_metrics.description: Short dramatic form historically used for quick, often punchline-driven pieces (credited to Euripides innovation; later film examples relied on quick punchlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suites shorter runtime and often require a quick punchline or compact structure; prescriptions are especially for short stories/short plays—must concentrate emotional arc and resolution tightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picaresque novel constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narrative by a lowborn protagonist ('pícaro') in a realistic setting; plot and character development is limited; often satiric tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural rule: episodic adventures with limited development—useful when aiming for satiric or episodic social critique rather than deep character evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bildungsroman requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative centered on a young or innocent protagonist who matures and learns about the world; the central goal is maturity of the protagonist achieved through discovery, conflict, or other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should support protagonist's psychological/social development; structure often follows apprenticeship/education arc culminating in integration into society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's unity and plot-focused tragedy rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly constructed plot is 'a whole' with a beginning, middle, and end; should imitate a single whole action (not episodic), often simple (prosperity → tragedy) to arouse pity and fear; discovery (anagnorisis) should be a high point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot ranks highest, followed by character, events/reason, diction, music, spectacle. Action should teach a moral reinforced by pity, fear, suffering. Recommends against episodic plots and for performability and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian stage divisions (prologue, episode, exode, parode, stasimon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle described stage portions such as Prologue, Episode, Exode, with choral portions Parode and Stasimon for structuring a play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinct stage portions for exposition, episodic action, and choral reflection; supports unity of action and performance conventions of classical drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid (five‑part dramatic arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot consists of five parts: Introduction (Exposition), Rise, Climax, Return or Fall, Catastrophe. Extended with optional crises: exciting force, tragic force, force of final suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freytag emphasizes emotional contrast and character centrality; the exciting force leads to the rise; tragic force leads to fall; final suspense leads to catastrophe. He views emotional juxtaposition as key; optionally include the three crises to expand to eight components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag — Introduction / Exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is fixed in a particular place and time, mood is set, and characters are introduced; backstory may be alluded to; exposition can be conveyed through dialogue, flashbacks, asides, background details, or narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exposition to establish setting, mood, and characters without delaying the exciting force; multiple techniques available—avoid info-dumps and keep focus on what will lead to the rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag — Rise (rising action / epitasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exciting force begins after the exposition, building the rise in stages toward the point of greatest interest; these events set up the climax and the satisfactory resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rise contains the most important plot events; should escalate stakes and complexity progressively to justify the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag — Climax (turning point/peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The turning point which changes the protagonist's fate; if things were going well they turn against the protagonist (or vice versa for comedy), often revealing hidden weaknesses or inner strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position the climax as the story's apex; the protagonist's choices/traits should be central to the turning point; for comedies the reversal moves from bad to good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag — Return or Fall (falling action / catabasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Return the counter-party's hostility beats upon the hero; Freytag's rules: limit number of characters as much as possible, and make the number of scenes in the fall fewer than in the rise; the return may contain a moment of final suspense and catastrophe must be foreshadowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constrained cast and compressed falling sequence; foreshadow catastrophe so it does not appear as a non sequitur; allow for a prospect of relief or final suspense before the outcome is inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag — Catastrophe (dénouement termination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The catastrophe is when the hero meets his logical destruction; Freytag warns the writer not to spare the life of the hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catastrophe should be the logical outcome of prior action and foreshadowing; do not rescue the hero in a way that undermines the plot's causal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kenneth Thorpe Rowe's dramatic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts: introduction, attack (inciting incident), rising action, crisis, falling action, resolution, conclusion. The 'attack' = inciting incident; 'crisis' = climax; Rowe centers conflict as the emotional core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension can continue after the turning point to the resolution; structure may be modified with extra complications; if a conclusion exists, make it shorter than the introduction; resolution can be a turning point distinct from climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lajos Egri: premise, character-driven conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues that character generates conflict, which generates events; emphasizes premise and the analysis of characters through physiology, sociology, and psychology; prefers rising conflict to reveal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design premise and characters so that their traits logically produce conflict and actions. Consider conflict types (static, jump, rise) and model attack/counterattack; use character internal logic over external plot imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syd Field's three‑act screenplay structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Act I: setup (first quarter) reveals main character, premise, and situation; Act II: confrontation (middle half) defines protagonist's main goal; Act III: resolution (final quarter) answers whether the protagonist succeeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear act breakpoints for turning points and midpoint beats; proportion screen-time as setup (25%), confrontation (50%), resolution (25%); useful for pacing and screenwriting format conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Northrop Frye's U-shaped and inverted U-shaped patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: U-shaped pattern = standard shape of comedy (decline then fortunate reversal to happy ending); inverted-U = tragedy (rise to prominence then crisis and descent to disaster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use U-shape for comedies where restoration of equilibrium is desired; inverted U for tragedies where reversal and downfall are central; recognizes recognition (anagnorisis) and peripety at the turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre of the Absurd structural anti‑pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays emphasizing the 'absurd' often lack formal plot structure, undercut conflict, mock human condition, and may leave things unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately subverts conventional structure—useful as an intentional anti-structure when the work's purpose is to convey meaninglessness or critique teleological plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative patterns (Jane Alison — Meander, Spiral, Explode)
rubrics_metrics.description: A criticism of conflict–climax–resolution as limiting; proposes narratives formed around natural patterns (meander, spiral, explode) instead of linear conflict arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages experimentation with non-linear or pattern-based forms that mirror natural processes; use when seeking alternatives to masculinized conflict-driven narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line of Emotion / graphical emotional arc (Whitcomb, Esenwein)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot elements tied to a 'line of emotion' (incident, emotion, crisis, suspense, climax, dénouement, conclusion) that can be graphed to represent reader emotion across the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for plotting emotional pacing in short stories; prioritize human interest and emotional rise—avoid flattening the emotional curve with irrelevant material; adapt curve shape to form length.
